bib.title: Efficient and Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Using Hierarchical Navigable Small World Graphs
bib.venue: IEEE Trans. Pattern Anal. Mach. Intell. 2020

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs", Yu. A. Malkov, D. A. Yashunin. arXiv 1603.09320. The PDF is the arXiv manuscript, headed "This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication". It is not the typeset IEEE TPAMI 2020 version.

COVERAGE: 70,413 of 70,413 chars, read in full: body, Algorithms 1 to 5, Tables 1 to 3, the text of the figure axes and legends, the discussion, the references and the bios. I skimmed the references for origins only. I did not run the figures script. The captions below come from the extracted text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Search complexity is O(log N). The proof assumes exact Delaunay graphs and a node degree capped by a constant. The approximate graph is supported only by simulations on low-dimensional data.
  number: O(log(N)); at most 1/(1-exp(-mL)) steps per layer
  setup: theory. The degree cap "is the case for random Euclid data [48], but can be in principle violated in exotic spaces"
  quote: "since the expectation of the maximum layer index by the construction scales as O(log(N)), the overall complexity scaling is O(log(N)), in agreement with the simulations on low dimensional datasets." / "the expected number of steps in a layer is bounded by a sum of geometric progression S =1/(1-exp(-mL)), which is independent of the dataset size."
  where: p.7, Section 4.2.1
- claim: Construction time scales as N log N, at least for low-dimensional data.
  number: O(N∙log(N))
  setup: relatively low-dimensional datasets
  quote: "at least for relatively low dimensional datasets the construction time scales as O(N∙log(N))."
  where: p.7, Section 4.2.2
- claim: NSW has polylogarithmic complexity because both the hop count and the hub degree grow logarithmically. HNSW splits links into layers by length scale, which caps the work per layer.
  number: none
  setup: analysis of the routing process
  quote: "the overall number of distance computations is roughly proportional to a product of the average number of greedy algorithm hops by the average degree of the nodes on the greedy path."
  where: p.3, Section 3
- claim: M is the only meaningful construction parameter left to the user. The reasonable range is 5 to 48. Small M suits low recall or low dimensions, and large M suits high recall or high dimensions. Memory grows in proportion to M.
  number: 5 to 48
  setup: Fig. 8, 5M SIFT, Core i5 2400
  quote: "The only meaningful construction parameter left for the user is M. A reasonable range of M is from 5 to 48." / "memory consumption of the algorithm (which is proportional to M)"
  where: p.6
- claim: The level normaliser mL defaults to 1/ln(M), which is the skip-list analogue p=1/M.
  number: mL = 1/ln(M)
  setup: Fig. 3: 10M random d=4 vectors, Core i7 5930K. Also Figs. 4 and 5 (d=1024, 5M SIFT)
  quote: "A simple choice for the optimal mL is 1/ln(M), this corresponds to the skip list parameter p=1/M with an average single element overlap between the layers."
  where: p.5, Section 4.1
- claim: Mmax0 (the maximum number of links on layer 0) should be 2·M. Setting it to M costs a lot at high recall. Setting it higher degrades performance and wastes memory.
  number: 2∙M
  setup: Fig. 6, 5M SIFT, M=20, Core i5 2400
  quote: "Simulations also suggest that 2∙M is a good choice for Mmax0: setting the parameter higher leads to performance degradation and excessive memory usage."
  where: p.6
- claim: efConstruction should be large enough that recall during construction is close to 1. Going higher adds little.
  number: 0.95 recall; efConstruction=100 builds 10M SIFT in 3 minutes
  setup: 10M SIFT, M=16, 4X 10-core Xeon E5-4650 v2, multithreaded
  quote: "it has to be large enough to produce K-ANNS recall close to unity during the construction process (0.95 is enough for the most use-cases)" / "a reasonable quality index can be constructed for efConstruction=100 on a 4X 2.4 GHz 10-core Xeon E5-4650 v2 CPU server in just 3 minutes."
  where: p.6-7
- claim: At query time, search quality is set by ef, the size of the dynamic candidate list on layer 0. The upper layers run with ef=1. The paper gives no recommended value for ef. Fig. 11 shows that the ef needed for a fixed recall saturates as N grows, for d=4.
  number: none
  setup: Algorithm 5; Fig. 11, random d=4, M=6
  quote: "The quality of the search is controlled by the ef parameter (corresponding to efConstruction in the construction algorithm)."
  where: p.5, p.7
- claim: The index (graph links, excluding the vectors) costs about 60 to 450 bytes per element, using 4-byte link IDs.
  number: (Mmax0+mL∙Mmax)∙bytes_per_link; 60 to 450 bytes per object
  setup: M from 6 to 48, fewer than about 4 billion elements
  quote: "the average memory consumption per element is (Mmax0+mL ∙Mmax)∙bytes_per_link" / "the typical memory requirements for the index (excluding the size of the data) are about 60-450 bytes per object"
  where: p.8, Section 4.2.3
- claim: In the 200M-SIFT comparison against Faiss PQ, HNSW used about twice the peak RAM but built far faster and gave higher accuracy and speed.
  number: HNSW 64 Gb, 5.6 h (efC=500) or 42 min (efC=40); Faiss 30 Gb, 12 h and 23.5 Gb, 11 h
  setup: 200M subset of 1B SIFT, 4X Xeon E5-4650 v2, 128 GB, Faiss May 2017 build, M=16
  quote: "Hierarchical NSW 5.6 hours 64 Gb M=16, efConstruction=500 (1) Hierarchical NSW 42 minutes 64 Gb M=16, efConstruction=40 (2) Faiss 12 hours 30 Gb OPQ64, IMI2x14, PQ64 (1) Faiss 11 hours 23.5 Gb OPQ32, IMI2x14, PQ32 (2)" / "Even though Hierarchical NSW requires significantly more RAM, it can achieve much higher accuracy, while offering a massive advance in search speed and much faster index construction."
  where: p.10-11, Table 3
- claim: On the ann-benchmark vector datasets, HNSW beats NSW, FLANN, Annoy, VP-tree and FALCONN by a large margin. On d=4 data it is only slightly faster than Annoy, and only at high recall. The results are curves; the paper gives no speedup figure.
  number: datasets: SIFT 1M/d128, GloVe 1.2M/d100, CoPhIR 2M/d272, random 30M/d4, DEEP 1M/d96, MNIST 60k/d784
  setup: single thread, 10-NN, 1,000 queries, best parameters per recall range, GCC -Ofast
  quote: "For SIFT, GloVE, DEEP and CoPhIR datasets Hierarchical NSW clearly outperforms the rivals by a large margin. For low dimensional data (d=4) Hierarchical NSW is slightly faster at high recall compared to the Annoy while strongly outperforms the other algorithms."
  where: p.8-9, Table 1, Fig. 13
- claim: In general (non-metric) spaces, HNSW leads on every dataset tested. Its largest gain over NSW, nearly 1,000x in distance computations, is on wiki-8 with JS divergence.
  number: "almost by 3 orders of magnitude"
  setup: nmslib tests from Naidan et al. [34]; Wiki-sparse, Wiki-8, Wiki-128, ImageNet SQFD, DNA Levenshtein; no custom distance functions
  quote: "The strongest enhancement over NSW, almost by 3 orders of magnitude is observed for the dataset with the lowest dimensionality, the wiki-8 with JS-divergence."
  where: p.10, Fig. 14
- claim: The diversity heuristic for choosing neighbours (Alg. 4) is never worse than taking the nearest neighbours (Alg. 3). Its gain is largest on low-dimensional data, at high recall, and on clustered data. Without it, search on clustered data gets stuck at cluster boundaries.
  number: none
  setup: Fig. 7, 10M d=10 random vectors with 100 clusters, M=16
  quote: "When using the closest neighbors as connections for the proximity graph, the Hierarchical NSW algorithm fails to achieve a high recall for clustered data because the search stucks at the clusters boundaries."
  where: p.6
- claim: NSW is the special case mL=0. HNSW search scales no worse than logarithmically and beats NSW at every dataset size tested.
  number: none
  setup: random hypercube data, d=8, 10-NN, recall 0.95
  quote: "Setting mL to zero and Mmax0 to infinity leads to production of NSW graphs with polylogarithmic complexity" / "Hierarchical NSW has a complexity scaling for this setting not worse than logarithmic and outperforms NSW at any dataset size."
  where: p.5, p.8

LIMITS
- The O(log N) proof needs an exact Delaunay graph. The authors concede that the real graph is approximate, that backtracking fills the gap, and that the evidence for this is empirical and only at d=4. Quote: "Further analitical evidence is required to confirm whether the resilience of Delaunay graph aproximations generalizes to higher dimensional spaces."
- On 200M SIFT the measured query time does not follow a pure logarithm. Quote: "the scaling deviates from the pure logarithm, possibly due to relatively high dimensionality of the dataset."
- The paper does not support deleting or updating elements. Quote: "add support for element updates and removal" (future work).
- Distributed search is lost compared with NSW. Quote: "One of the apparent shortcomings of the proposed approach compared to the basic NSW is the loss of the possibility of distributed search."
- The memory cost is high: twice the RAM of Faiss PQ in Table 3. The per-element estimate excludes the vectors themselves.
- The paper does not show:
  - a recommended value for ef at query time
  - results on full billion-scale data (1B SIFT or DEEP is left as future work)
  - GPU baselines
  - Filtered or hybrid search
  - a quantised or compressed HNSW
- Dated:
  - The baselines are 2016-17 builds: Annoy 02.02.2016, FLANN 1.8.4, FALCONN 1.2, Faiss May 2017.
  - A footnote says "From 2018 Faiss library has its own implementation of Hierarchical NSW."

BUILDS ON
- NSW: Malkov, Ponomarenko, Logvinov, Krylov 2012 and 2014 [25, 26], and Ponomarenko et al. 2011 [30]
- Skip list: Pugh 1990 [27]
- Navigable small worlds: Kleinberg 2000 [31, 41], and Boguna, Krioukov, Claffy 2009 [32]
- Spatial approximation tree, the source of the heuristic: Navarro 2002 [4]
- Relative neighbourhood graph: Toussaint 1980 [46]
- Sparse neighbourhood graphs: Arya and Mount 1993 [18]
- Concurrent heuristic: FANNG, Harwood and Drummond 2016 [47]
- k-NN graph construction: Dong, Moses, Li 2011 [29], NNDescent
- Implementation in nmslib: Boytsov and Naidan 2013 [49]

CODE
- Algorithm 1, line 4, random level: "l ← ⌊-ln(unif(0..1))∙mL⌋  // new element's level" (p.4)
- Algorithm 4, core rule of the heuristic: "if e is closer to q compared to any element from R / R ← R ⋃ e / else / Wd ← Wd ⋃ e" (p.5)
- Algorithm 5, search: "for lc ← L … 1 / W ← SEARCH-LAYER(q, ep, ef=1, lc) / ep ← get nearest element from W to q / W ← SEARCH-LAYER(q, ep, ef, lc =0) / return K nearest elements from W to q" (p.5)
- Algorithm 2, stop rule: "if distance(c, q) > distance(f, q) break // all elements in W are evaluated" (p.4)
- Reference implementations: https://github.com/nmslib/hnsw and nmslib

FIGURES
- Fig. 1, p.3: "Illustration of the Hierarchical NSW idea. The search starts from an element from the top layer..." It shows the layered greedy descent at a glance, so it fits the note's HNSW section.
- Fig. 2, p.3: the heuristic keeps a link to the other cluster (e2). It shows why taking only the nearest neighbours breaks connectivity.
- Fig. 8, p.6: recall error vs query time for M from 2 to 40 on 5M SIFT. It shows the trade-off in choosing M.
- Fig. 10, p.7: query time vs build time, which is the efConstruction trade-off.
- Fig. 12, p.8: distance computations for NSW vs HNSW as dataset size grows. It shows polylogarithmic vs logarithmic scaling.
- Fig. 13, p.9: recall vs query time against Annoy, FLANN, VP-tree and FALCONN. This is the direct source for the note's "HNSW vs. ANNOY" comparison.
- Fig. 15, p.10: HNSW vs Faiss on 200M SIFT.

PROBLEMS
- The extraction inserts hyphenation splits such as "co n-nections" and "Hiera r-chical". I repaired these in the quotes only where a word was split. I kept the source's own spellings ("stucks", "cognestion").
- The plot axes come out as loose numbers, so values cannot be read off the curves. The comparison claims are therefore qualitative.
- The PDF is the arXiv preprint, not the TPAMI 2020 version, so cite page numbers carefully.
- The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
